Retrieval-Augmented Generation pairs a language model with a non-parametric
memory: a document index it can query at inference time. Instead of relying
solely on facts baked into its weights during training, the model retrieves
a small set of relevant passages for the current question and conditions its
answer on them. This lets a model answer questions about information it was
never trained on, and lets that information be updated by editing the index
rather than retraining the model.

A typical RAG pipeline has two stages. The retriever encodes the question
and every candidate passage into a shared vector space, usually with a dense
encoder trained so that a question's embedding lands close to the embeddings
of passages that answer it, then returns the top-scoring passages by cosine
or dot-product similarity. The generator, usually a sequence-to-sequence or
decoder-only language model, then reads the question together with the
retrieved passages and produces the final answer, often with the retrieved
text spliced directly into the prompt.

Dense retrieval alone can miss passages that share exact keywords with the
question but sit far from it in embedding space, particularly for rare
terms, identifiers, or exact phrases. Combining a dense retriever with a
sparse, keyword-based retriever like BM25 and fusing their rankings —
commonly with Reciprocal Rank Fusion — tends to recover more relevant
passages than either retriever alone, since the two make different kinds of
mistakes.

Because retrieval quality bounds answer quality, later work added a
correction step: grade the retrieved passages for relevance before
generating, and fall back to a broader search — even the open web — when
the retrieved set is too weak to support an answer. This turns a single
retrieve-then-generate pass into a small decision loop, which is the core
idea behind corrective retrieval-augmented generation.
